You tell the story of a trip: where you went, when you left and arrived, with the passé composé with être.
I went to Paris on Saturday. (woman)
She went up to the top of the Eiffel Tower.
To know which verbs take ÊTRE in the passé composé (the “house” verbs).
To make the participle agree with the subject: elle est allée, ils sont partis.
To put reflexive verbs in the past: je me suis levé(e).
To choose between AVOIR and ÊTRE.
To tell the story of a train journey.
Ioana and Julien spent a day in Paris for an architecture exhibition. On Sunday evening Madame Bernard meets them on the stairs.
Good evening, young people! Are you back from Paris?
Yes, we got back an hour ago. What a day!
Very early! I got up at five. The TGV left at ten past six.
And I arrived at the station late! Julien waited for me on the platform.
She got on the train thirty seconds before it left!
Ha ha! And in Paris, what did you do?
In the morning we went to the exhibition. In the afternoon we visited the Louvre.
Then we went up to the top of the Eiffel Tower. Ioana was a bit scared!
A bit, yes! But the view is incredible. Afterwards we walked down and strolled along the Seine.
How romantic! I only went to Paris once, in 1975. I stayed three days and it rained the whole time.
We were lucky: it was nice all day.
And Victor? He went out this morning and he hasn’t come back yet…
Don’t worry. He’s surely gone to the café on Place Saint-Jean. He loves croissants!
are (“vous êtes rentrés” = you came back)
am (“je me suis levé” = I got up)
top (“en haut de” = at the top of)
walked (“nous nous sommes promenés” = we strolled)
bank (“au bord de” = along, on the bank of)
All forms of the participle sound the same: allé, allée, allés, allées = “a-LAY”. Agreement only shows in writing.
Same here: parti, partie, partis = “par-TEE”. Only a few participles sound different in the feminine: mis / mise (“mee / meez”), pris / prise (“pree / preez”).
Don’t mix up the auxiliaries: “je suis allé” = “zhuh swee a-LAY”, “j’ai mangé” = “zhay mahn-ZHAY”. Listen to the first sound after the subject.
Liaison: “vous êtes arrivés” = “voo-zet-a-ree-VAY”, “ils sont allés” = “eel sõ-ta-LAY”. You hear the linking t.
Eiffel = “ay-FEL”, stressed on the last syllable, like all French words. Louvre = “loovr”, Seine = “sen”.
1. Verbs with ÊTRE: the “house of verbs”
In the passé composé, a small list of verbs uses ÊTRE instead of AVOIR. English has nothing like this: we say “I have gone”, the French say “I am gone”: “je suis allé”.
They are mostly verbs of MOVEMENT from one place to another. You can learn them like a house: you go in, up, down, out…
And their derivatives: revenir → revenu, devenir → devenu (to become), repartir → reparti.
Careful: “marcher” (to walk), “courir” (to run), “voyager” (to travel) are also about movement, but they take AVOIR: “j’ai marché”, “j’ai voyagé”. The ÊTRE list is short and fixed: learn it.
With ÊTRE, the participle agrees with the subject, like an adjective: +e for feminine, +s for plural.
il est allé / elle est allée
ils sont allés / elles sont allées

Ioana, being a woman, always writes “je suis allée, je suis arrivée”. In the dialogue, “nous sommes arrivés” has an -s because there are two of them (Ioana + Julien): a mixed group takes the masculine plural.
With AVOIR the participle does NOT agree with the subject: “elle a mangé” (not “mangée”). Agreement only happens with ÊTRE.
ALL reflexive verbs (chapter 6) take ÊTRE in the passé composé. The reflexive pronoun comes before the auxiliary:
il s’est levé / elle s’est levée
ils se sont levés / elles se sont levées
Negation: ne + pronoun + auxiliary + pas + participle: “Je ne me suis pas réveillée” (I didn’t wake up).
Literally “je me suis levé” = “I am myself got up”. Odd in English, but the pattern is always the same.
4. AVOIR or ÊTRE? How to choose
→ AVOIR: j’ai visité, j’ai pris, j’ai marché.
Compare them in the same story:
We went to the Louvre and saw the Mona Lisa.
She went out and bought some bread.
The weather takes AVOIR: “il a plu” (it rained, from pleuvoir), “il a neigé” (it snowed).
TGV = Train à Grande Vitesse (high-speed train). Between Lyon and Paris it takes only two hours for 450 km.
Did you go for a walk?
marcher isn’t in the “house of verbs”.
Julien s’est levé à quelle heure ?
Ioana est arrivée à la gare…
Madame Bernard est allée à Paris…
One Friday in November, Radu, Ioana’s little brother, came to Lyon for the first time. He took the plane from Iași at six in the morning.
But the journey was long. First he went to Munich. There his second plane left two hours late.
Ioana arrived at the airport at noon. She waited. One hour, two hours, three hours… She drank three coffees and read a whole newspaper.
Finally, at three pm, Radu came out with an enormous rucksack. “Hi, sis! I’m starving!”
They went back into town by tram. Radu looked out of the window the whole time. “It’s beautiful here! More beautiful than on TV!”
On Saturday they went up Fourvière, the hill with the big white basilica. They stayed at the top for an hour, looking at the view over the whole city.
Then they walked down through the little streets of Vieux Lyon. Radu went into every sweet shop.
In the evening Julien came for dinner. Radu and Julien talked about football for two hours, in English, in French and with their hands.
On Sunday morning Ioana woke up early. Radu wasn’t in the living room! She went out onto the landing, worried.
Madame Bernard’s door was open. Radu was there, sitting in the kitchen, with Victor on his lap and a croissant in his hand.
“Hello, Ioana!” said Madame Bernard. “Your brother came down at seven. He speaks very bad French, but he eats very well!”
knees (“sur les genoux” = on his lap)
Le deuxième avion de Radu est parti…

Write 8–10 sentences in French about a trip you’ve made: where you went, when you left and arrived, how, what you visited, what you ate, when you came back. Mix verbs with AVOIR and ÊTRE and make the participles agree. You can also write a postcard, like Ioana. Useful verbs: visiter (avoir), voyager (avoir), se baigner (to swim in the sea, être), se promener (être), tomber (être), découvrir → découvert (avoir).
